**Analyzing Premise 1: ((S ∨ P) ↔ (S ↔ P))**

Let me evaluate all possible truth values for S and P:

| S | P | S∨P | S↔P | (S∨P)↔(S↔P) |
|---|---|-----|-----|--------------|
| T | T |  T  |  T  |      T       |
| T | F |  T  |  F  |      F       |
| F | T |  T  |  F  |      F       |
| F | F |  F  |  T  |      F       |

The biconditional in premise 1 is **true only when S = T and P = T**. Therefore, premise 1 forces us to conclude **S ∧ P**.

**Analyzing Premise 2: (R ↔ Q)**

This directly tells us R ↔ Q.

**Combining both conclusions:**

From premise 1: S ∧ P
From premise 2: R ↔ Q

The combined conclusion is:

<answer>(S ∧ P) ∧ (R ↔ Q)</answer>
